title: Service economics & latency claim matrix: playsheet for field and content
summary: Operational playbook for making defensible latency + cost claims in sales and marketing. Includes measurable proof points, benchmark protocol, customer math templates, objection handling, and required collateral.
content:
Purpose and intended use:
This is a lightweight playsheet for field reps, content writers, and product marketing to craft defensible statements about Redwood’s performance and unit economics (latency, cost per inference, throughput). Primary goals: 1) have repeatable benchmark language that’s easy to communicate; 2) provide reproducible evidence for claims; 3) give quick math templates for customer conversations and RFPs.

High-level positioning summary (one-liners to test):
- “Same quality, 2–5x lower per-request cost at 99th-percentile latency targets.”
- “Predictable throughput, linear scaling, and automatic fallbacks keep production traffic within cost targets.”
- "Reduce token spend by 20–60% via KV/prefix caching and optimized batching without adding latency."

What we mean by “unit economics” here:
- Unit = a single customer request as observed by the app (a chat turn or a prompt).
- Cost components: compute (GPU time), memory/IO (KV-cache hits), networking egress, orchestration overhead (scheduling, retries).
- Latency SLOs expressed as p50/p95/p99 end-to-end (api ingress -> final token).
- Throughput measured as sustained requests per second at target latency SLO.

Benchmark claim categories (with safe language templates):
- Latency leadership (p95/p99): “In our public benchmarks Redwood serves conversational models at p95 = X ms, p99 = Y ms for 1kB median prompts on N1 instances.”
- Cost per request: “Typical production workloads see $A–$B per 1000 requests (median), driven by batching and prefix cache.”
- Throughput density: “One Dedicated pod sustains T requests/sec at p95 < L ms for a mixed chat workload.”
- Quality-preserving efficiency: “After applying quantization and low-latency kernels, output quality (BLEU/ROUGE or human eval) is unchanged within 1–2%.”

Benchmark methodology (short, reproducible):
- Workload definitions: 1) Chat micro (short prompts 200–600 tokens), 2) Assistant long-form (1k–2k tokens), 3) Embeddings batch (256–512 vectors).
- Test harness: use the redwood-bench repo (linked in artifacts) with fixed seeds, identical tokenizer, and same model versions across vendors.
- Environment: Dedicated GPU (A100/80GB equiv) and Hosted (n1-standard equivalent) runs to show hosted vs dedicated delta. Note instance details in every test.
- Measurement: collect p50/p95/p99 latency; GPU utilization; tokens/s; cost estimate using our internal GPU-minute-to-dollar model.
- Caching enabled/disabled: report both numbers. For public claims default to “with default KV/prefix caching enabled” unless otherwise stated.
- Repeatability: run 3x across separate 30-minute windows; report median.

Concrete proof points to collect and standardize (examples we should have by EOW):
- Micro-chat: p95 = 85ms, cost/request = $0.0023 (example target).
- Long-form: p95 = 210ms, cost/request = $0.009.
- Embeddings (batched): 5k vectors/sec per pod, cost/vector = $0.00001.
Note: these are placeholders. Replace with validated results and tag with environment, model, and date.

Customer math templates (quick fill for SDRs/AE):
1) Baseline customer: 1M chat turns/month, median prompt = 400 tokens.
2) Redwood delivered: average cost/req = $0.003. Monthly cost = 1,000,000 * 0.003 = $3,000.
3) Competitor baseline (public pricing or customer supplied): average cost/req = $0.01; monthly cost = $10,000.
4) Savings = $7,000/mo or 70% lower.
Add notes: include soft savings from fewer timeouts, lower tail latency leading to increased user engagement, and fewer retries.

How we’re faster/cheaper — engineering levers to cite (short bullets for sales):
- Adaptive batching: dynamically bundles compatible requests to reach higher GPU utilization while capping added queuing latency.
- Prefix & KV cache: avoids re-computing prefixes for multi-turn chats; common customer patterns yield 20–60% token reductions.
- Model routing & fallbacks: route to smaller quantized variants when latency or capacity constraints appear, maintaining SLA.
- Kernel/compilation tuning: per-model kernel selection to reduce per-token latency by avoiding generic operators.
- Dedicated capacity: avoids noisy neighbors, reduces p99 spikes seen on shared endpoints.

Competitor callouts (framing guidance, don't invent numbers for public claims):
- Don’t name competitors in public collateral unless figures are from verifiable public docs.
- In sales calls, use compare/contrast: “Other hosted endpoints optimize for throughput at the cost of p99—our offering flips that tradeoff by prioritizing latency SLOs with cost controls.”

Objection handling (common field pushback + suggested responses):
- "Your numbers sound synthetic": Response: “We publish our benchmark protocol and can run a quick pilot using your sample prompts to validate in <72 hours.”
- "We already use model X on MajorCloud": Response: “We can show a side-by-side using your trace; common outcomes: reduced tail latency and 20–40% per-request GPU-minutes due to caching and batching.”
- "Quantization will reduce quality": Response: “We gate quantized variants behind evals; for most assistant workflows your NRR/CTR-quality signals are unchanged within measurement error.”

Collateral required (assets to finalize before broad distribution):
- One-pager: 2x claims (latency & cost) with explicit measurement notes.
- Slide deck: benchmark protocol slide, customer math page, reproducibility appendix.
- Customer playbook: step-by-step how to run an in-house pilot.
- Short demo script: 6-minute demo focusing on latency and TCO.
- Public benchmark page: interactive tables for p50/p95/p99 and per-request cost (tied to model version/date).

A/B test ideas for messaging (what to try in email/website):
- Variant A: emphasize percent savings (“Cut inference costs by up to 70%”)
- Variant B: emphasize latency SLOs (“Consistent sub-100ms p95 for conversational workloads”)
- Variant C: emphasize predictable capacity (“Reserve Dedicated pods and guarantee throughput”)
Measure CTR, demo bookings, and technical trial opt-ins.

Regulatory/compliance notes (to include in claims):
- For enterprise customers in regulated industries, collect validation when claiming numbers for Private deployments — hosted numbers may not match VPC/on-prem profiles.
- Always append model/regression test IDs for claims tied to quality.

Next steps and owners:
- PM (Maya Chen): validate three benchmark runs for micro-chat and long-form by 2025-02-10.
- SRE (Oliver Greene): generate reproducible runbook and link to artifacts.
- GTM (Aisha Khan + Rajiv Patel): draft one-pager and demo script by 2025-02-24.
- Field pilot: target 2 Customer pilots in verticals (SaaS and FinServ) by end of Q1; capture customer traces for apples-to-apples comparison.

Appendix: quick checklist for public claims
- show environment, model version, date
- show whether caching/batching was enabled
- include p50/p95/p99 and cost estimation method
- link to reproducibility repo or offer to run a pilot

End notes:
This doc is intentionally prescriptive and lightweight. The purpose is to reduce variability in field statements and make any ROI claim immediately actionable and auditable. Keep language conservative in external collateral; field teams can use richer math in private sales decks and pilots.
